Greek: Τὰ αὐτὰ λέγειν ὑμῖν matches Philippians 3:1 'To write the same things to you'
Concept of striving toward a goal (skopon) resembles Paul’s athletic metaphor for spiritual discipline
Phrase 'from above' (ἄνωθεν) echoes James 1:17 'every good gift... comes down from the Father of lights'
Contrast between holiness and Gentile depravity aligns with Paul’s call to separation from uncleanness

choices.why: The noun ὠνίνησις conveys benefit or advantage; context shows it refers to the value of righteous deeds observed by others.
The adverb modifies the divine response to prayer; it contrasts God’s prompt attention to the righteous with His delayed response to others, as clarified in the following clause.
The participle describes those who stand out in righteousness; literal ‘shine through’ is metaphorical, so ‘conspicuous’ captures the sense of visible virtue in context.
The genitive ἀνός modifies a state of absence; ‘without longing’ fits the sense of eager, unimpeded prayer, contrasting with delay or hesitation.
The verb implies active reaching; God extends toward the petitions of the righteous, so ‘stretches out’ conveys initiative better than ‘grants’ or ‘gives’.
The superlative adjective modifies ἀκοὴν (hearing); God’s attentiveness is not just willing but fully prepared, so ‘most ready’ heightens the sense of immediacy.
The adverb modifies μετὰ σοῦ (with you); it expresses continual divine presence, not just frequent or perpetual in a vague sense.
Contextually fits Paul’s ethical contrast; 'corruption' or 'baseness' are possible but less precise for moral decay in Gentile practices.
Standard ecclesiastical term in early Christian Greek for appointed ministry; 'selection' or 'appointment' are weaker ecclesiastically.
Direct semantic rendering; 'greed' or 'avarice' are broader and miss the specific act of seeking bribes.

pass_b_english: The usefulness of righteous deeds is not moderate for those who see them. Indeed, Christ said to his holy apostles: ‘Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.’ Therefore, we shall be radiant, carried about and as it were clothed with the glory from God, to those to whom he might grant justice as caretakers.

Having existed for you, he says, you will cry out then, and God will hear you. Even while you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Behold, I have come.’ For the prayer of the righteous he hears, as it is written. And as the Melodist says: ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their petition.’ He nods indeed to those who ask, as a good God, but not to all immediately.

To those, however, who have been conspicuous in righteousness, without any longing, he stretches out their petitions and holds most ready their hearing, so that, in regard to each of their requests, they rejoice and say: ‘He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry entered into his ears.’ Thus, the surpassing earnestness of ambition, and the very readiness of the giving God, are plainly set forth in the cry, ‘Behold, I have come,’ still speaking of the righteous, stretching out their petitions.

If you remove from yourself bond, hand-raising, and murmuring speech, and give your bread to the hungry, and satisfy the humbled soul, then your light will rise in the darkness, and your darkness will be at noon, and your God will be with you always. The exceptional lessons, even if often said to some, nevertheless have their usefulness.

The all-wise Paul writes to those who came to faith through him, saying that repeating the same teachings is no burden to him but is for their safety. Thus, through these same teachings, he speaks to us in many ways, making clear the paths to success and recounting the joy of the gifts promised to the saints, so that he might stir us to greater zeal in doing the deeds by which we may become venerable, and we shall discover the ambition that comes from above and from him.

Therefore, he says, 'If you remove from yourselves a bond and an ordination.' And by bond he means, as I understand, the depravity of the nations, their shamelessness, their love of strife, and the practice of forming alliances against others for selfish ends, as well as inventing crooked schemes to entrap people, sometimes binding them with fetters and bringing upon them helpless circumstances.

For a person must be simple and approachable if they are to look toward God and cling to the graces that come from him. But by ordination he perhaps means, in some places, the love of bribes and the pursuit of shameful gain, which we do indeed sometimes observe.
